cfaa-1030a2.statute: 18 U.S.C. § 1030(a)(2) -- Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (federal)
cfaa-1030a2.plain_language: Intentionally accessing a computer without authorization, or exceeding authorized access, and thereby obtaining information from a protected computer. The SQL-injection login bypass is exactly this: the attacker never had valid credentials, tricked the login query into authenticating them anyway, and obtained account information as a result.
elements: without authorization, or exceeding authorized access
obtaining information from a protected computer
cfaa-1030a2.penalty: Under 18 U.S.C. § 1030(c)(2): baseline misdemeanor, up to 1 year. It becomes a felony, up to 5 years, if the access was for commercial advantage or private financial gain, in furtherance of any criminal or tortious act, OR the value obtained exceeds $5,000 -- and up to 10 years on a repeat offense. Verified 2026-08-28 against the House OLRC statute text and the U.S. Sentencing Commission's 2021 Computer Crimes primer.
cfaa-1030a2.case_law: Van Buren v. United States, 141 S. Ct. 1648 (2021): the CFAA reaches accessing files/areas that are off-limits to you -- a defeated login (SQLi bypass, brute-forced SSH, a triggered backdoor shell) is squarely covered even under this narrowed reading. United States v. Morris, 928 F.2d 504 (2d Cir. 1991): the first CFAA conviction (the 'Morris Worm') -- the government need only prove intent to ACCESS without authorization, not intent to cause the damage that followed; the key precedent for holding whoever launches autonomous code liable for the access it makes.
cfaa-1030a2.evidentiary_note: The proxy's access log entry capturing the exact injection payload in the login request body is the kind of artifact that establishes intent -- this wasn't a fat-fingered password, it's a crafted attempt to manipulate the query.

co-18-5.5-102.statute: Colo. Rev. Stat. § 18-5.5-102 -- Colorado Computer Crime Act (state)
co-18-5.5-102.plain_language: Colorado's own computer-crime statute, prosecuted far more often in practice than federal CFAA cases. Using the bypassed session to pull other users' full account records via /api/Users/{id} -- which authenticates the caller but never checks whether that record actually belongs to them -- is unauthorized access to, and use of, data the attacker was never entitled to see.
elements: knowingly accessing a computer, network, or data without authorization
use of that access to obtain data, or additional access
co-18-5.5-102.penalty: C.R.S. § 18-5.5-102: bare unauthorized access is a class 2 misdemeanor (up to 120 days); a second conviction becomes a class 6 felony (1 to 1.5 years). Where a loss/value figure applies, Colorado tiers it -- under $500: class 2 misdemeanor; $500 to $1,000: class 1 misdemeanor (up to 364 days); $1,000 to $20,000: class 4 felony (2-6 years + 3 years mandatory parole, fine $2,000-$500,000); $20,000+: class 3 felony (4-12 years + 3 years mandatory parole, fine $3,000-$750,000). Prison ranges reflect current post-SB21-271 sentencing (C.R.S. § 18-1.3-401), verified 2026-08-28; treat exact fine caps as practitioner-sourced. Which tier fits exposed personal data is itself an argument -- flag it live rather than asserting one number.
co-18-5.5-102.case_law: No controlling Colorado appellate decision squarely defines 'without authorization' on these facts, and in practice this state statute is charged far more often than federal CFAA. Van Buren's federal 'off-limits areas' reasoning (141 S. Ct. 1648 (2021)) is persuasive, not binding, authority for the enumeration step -- the records pulled were areas the attacker was never entitled to reach.
co-18-5.5-102.evidentiary_note: The detector's alert -- three or more distinct user IDs pulled via the same session within a 10-second window -- is the kind of access pattern that distinguishes 'looked up my own account' from systematic enumeration, which matters for proving intent.

cfaa-1030a2-misconfig.statute: 18 U.S.C. § 1030(a)(2) -- Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (federal) -- unauthenticated-exposure fact pattern
cfaa-1030a2-misconfig.plain_language: Same statute as the SQLi bypass above, but a genuinely more contested fact pattern worth surfacing to a criminal-justice audience: no login was bypassed, no technical control was defeated -- the file simply had no access control on it at all. Courts have split on whether requesting a URL with no authentication barrier is 'without authorization' under the CFAA (see, e.g., the vacated AT&T/Weev iPad-URL case) versus whether it's closer to leaving a folder on a public sidewalk. This step is deliberately the 'weakest' legal case in the chain -- a good discussion prompt, not a slam dunk.
elements: without authorization -- contested here, since no credential or technical barrier was ever in place
cfaa-1030a2-misconfig.penalty: Same 18 U.S.C. § 1030(c)(2) range as cfaa-1030a2 IF charged -- but prosecutorial discretion and case law both trend against charging pure unauthenticated access where no barrier was ever defeated. Present this step's exposure with less confidence than a defeated-control step.
cfaa-1030a2-misconfig.case_law: United States v. Auernheimer ('weev'), 748 F.3d 525 (3d Cir. 2014): a conviction for collecting AT&T's publicly-reachable iPad email addresses via guessable URLs was VACATED (on venue), leaving the core question -- is accessing a resource with no authentication barrier 'without authorization'? -- unresolved. Van Buren's 'gates-up-or-down' framing (141 S. Ct. 1648 (2021)) cuts toward the defense here: no gate was ever closed. Deliberately the chain's weakest legal case.
cfaa-1030a2-misconfig.evidentiary_note: The proxy log shows a single unauthenticated GET with a 200 response -- there's no crafted payload, no bypassed check, just a request to a path that should never have been reachable. That absence of any 'attack artifact' is itself the point for this step.

identity-theft-1028.statute: 18 U.S.C. § 1028 / § 1028A (federal) and Colo. Rev. Stat. § 18-5-902 (state) -- Identity Theft
identity-theft-1028.plain_language: Resetting another person's password via a guessable security question and logging in as them is textbook identity theft -- using another person's identifying information/account access without their permission to obtain something of value (here: full control of their account). Federal § 1028A adds a mandatory, non-discretionary 2-year sentence on top of whatever the underlying felony carries, served consecutively -- judges cannot reduce or run it concurrently. Colorado's § 18-5-902 is the state-level version, prosecuted independently or alongside federal charges.
elements: knowingly uses another person's personal identifying information or account access
to obtain something of value (here: account control) -- or, for the federal aggravated charge, in relation to another listed felony
identity-theft-1028.penalty: Colorado § 18-5-902: class 4 felony -- 2 to 6 years prison, 3 years mandatory parole, fine $2,000-$500,000; prison is mandatory on a qualifying prior. Federal § 1028A: a mandatory 2-year sentence served CONSECUTIVELY to the underlying felony -- a judge cannot suspend it, reduce it, or run it concurrently. Colorado prison ranges verified 2026-08-28 against current C.R.S. § 18-1.3-401; § 1028A's mandatory-consecutive structure is on the face of the statute.
identity-theft-1028.case_law: Flores-Figueroa v. United States, 556 U.S. 646 (2009): a unanimous Supreme Court held § 1028A's 'knowingly ... a means of identification of ANOTHER PERSON' requires the government to prove the defendant KNEW the identity belonged to a real person. Easy here -- the attacker targeted a specific named user (jim@juice-sh.op) -- but this becomes the crux the moment an AI, not a human, picks the victim: whose knowledge satisfies the statute?
identity-theft-1028.evidentiary_note: The proxy log shows the exact sequence: a security-question lookup, a successful reset (200, not the 401 a wrong guess gets), then a login with the new credentials -- a clean, hard-to-dispute timeline of exactly how the takeover happened.

co-6-1-716.statute: Colo. Rev. Stat. § 6-1-716 -- Notification of Security Breach (state, civil/regulatory)
co-6-1-716.plain_language: Not a charge against the attacker -- this is what the law now requires of the breached organization. Once personal information (like the emails and roles just pulled) is confirmed accessed without authorization, Colorado law obligates the company to notify affected residents.
elements: unauthorized acquisition of unencrypted personal information
compromising its security, confidentiality, or integrity
co-6-1-716.penalty: Not a criminal penalty on the attacker -- a notification duty on the victim organization under C.R.S. § 6-1-716: notice 'in the most expedient time possible... but not later than 30 days' after the breach is confirmed (among the strictest deadlines in the U.S.), plus notice to consumer reporting agencies if over 1,000 Colorado residents are affected. Verified 2026-08-28.
co-6-1-716.evidentiary_note: This is the moment the incident stops being purely a technical/criminal question and becomes an organizational-response question too -- useful pivot point for the law-enforcement track: what happens after the arrest/charges, on the victim side.
